### Webpage: https://safe.engr.tamu.edu Biography

Dr. Nancy Currie-Gregg is the Director of the Texas A&M University Space Institute. As the Don Lummus '58 Professor of Practice in Engineering, she holds joint appointments in the Departments of Aerospace Engineering and Industrial and Systems Engineering at Texas A&M University's College of Engineering. Internationally recognized for her human-system integration, safety engineering, and risk management expertise, her research focuses on optimizing human performance and safety in aerospace systems. She also serves on the Board of Directors for the Texas Space Commission, leading initiatives that promote growth across all sectors of the Texas space economy.

Dr. Currie-Gregg spent the majority of her career supporting NASA's human spaceflight programs. A former NASA astronaut, she flew on four space shuttle missions, logging over 1,000 hours in space, and made significant contributions to the development of human spaceflight operations. Following the Space Shuttle Columbia tragedy, she managed the Space Shuttle Program Safety and Mission Assurance Office, overseeing the agency's return-to-flight efforts. She later served as Principal Engineer and Chief Engineer with the NASA Engineering and Safety Center, where she led independent engineering assessments for high-risk human spaceflight initiatives. A retired U.S. Army Colonel and Master Army Aviator, she accrued more than 4,000 flight hours in both rotary- and fixed-wing aircraft.

Dr. Currie-Gregg holds a Bachelor's degree in Biological Sciences with honors from The Ohio State University, a Master of Science in Safety Engineering from the University of Southern California, and a Ph.D. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Houston.

## Catalog Description

Human Factors Engineering for Aerospace Designs. (3-0). Credit 3. Physiological and psychophysiological issues encountered in aviation and space environments and their effect on human cognitive and physical performance; survey methods for human workload and performance evaluations; apply human-systems design principles to an aerospace design project. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with AERO 636.

## Additional Course Details

This course is designated as an online, distance learning course. It will be conducted concurrently with a 'face-to-face' course on the Texas A&M University campus. Distance students may participate in the course synchronously, via Zoom, during the scheduled lecture periods on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 09:35-10:50 a.m. or 11:10 a.m.- 12:25 p.m. CT. Students should contact the instructor 24 hours in advance of the lecture period to attend via Zoom. Only students registered in 700-sections of the course may exercise this option.

Alternatively, distance-learning students whose work schedules preclude synchronous participation in lectures may choose to take the course asynchronously. All lectures will be recorded and available the same day.

Due to the pace of the course, distance students must be diligent about watching the recorded lectures per the course schedule and adhere to the scheduled due dates for all assignments and exams. All distance learning students are expected to keep up with the pace of the course by watching the lecture recordings and completing any lecture activities within three days of the recording date. All course deliverables for distance-learning students will be submitted electronically through the course Canvas site.

For any lab activities, distance-learning students will be provided with de-identified data in order to complete all assignments. Recordings of the lab activities will also be uploaded to Canvas.

## Course Learning Outcomes

Upon completion of this course, the learner will be able to:

- Analyze how human sensory, motor, and cognitive attributes may influence human performance in the operation of aviation and space systems.

- Discuss principle physiological and psychophysiological concerns related to aviation and spaceflight environments and evaluate their potential impact on human performance.

- Formulate and evaluate principled hypotheses for human-system design optimization and improvement.

- Critique published literature on physiological and psychophysiological issues and evaluate proposed mitigations and countermeasures.

- Develop solutions to current human-system integration challenges for aerospace applications.

- Assess proposed design solutions from the perspective of human performance to include physical/cognitive workload, attention, situation awareness, and mission performance.

- Synthesize and effectively communicate attributes of the proposed design solutions to include specific human-system integration requirements, system characteristics, and human performance assessment results.

## Special Course Designation

None

This is a cross-listed course with both AERO and ISEN sections due to the interdisciplinary nature of the subject. It is also stacked with the undergraduate versions of the course (AERO 436/ISEN 432). Graduate and undergraduate students will have different requirements and weighting for quizzes, homework assignments, and the course project.

#### Lecture Activities

Class attendance and participation are the individual responsibility of each student. Students are expected to attend all lectures and participate in the learning process unless they have a university-approved absence (see Student Rule 7).

This course will use active learning methods, such as group activities, discussions, surveys, and experiential learning, to encourage student engagement in their learning. The points for each lecture activity will vary, with those associated with experiential learning opportunities having the most points.

All lecture activities must be completed in class and may not be submitted late unless the instructor has granted an extension due to a pre-approved universityexcused absence. If a student misses an activity due to a university-excused absence (see Student Rule 7), and has notified the instructor, in writing, in advance of the absence, they may receive an extension to the lecture activity submission deadline.

chunks.content:
#### Quizzes

There will be four quizzes throughout the semester. The detailed schedule denotes what material will be covered on each quiz.

Quizzes for distance-learning students will be administered on the same day as the on-campus quiz. The quiz time will be determined by polling distance-learning students and selecting an evening time that accommodates working students. All quizzes will be proctored by the instructor or GTA.

#### Homework

There will be approximately five homework assignments during the semester. Detailed instructions for each homework assignment, including due dates and times and the maximum possible points for each assignment element, will be provided on the course Canvas site and discussed during lectures.

Some homework assignments will also be designated as 'design competitions.' Students who present superior solutions for the assignment will be awarded extra credit points, which will be applied to the homework grade.

#### Course Project

A crucial aspect of the course is participation in a group project to design an aircraft or spacecraft system that enhances operator effectiveness, usability, and safety. This project aims to deepen comprehension and understanding by applying course concepts and methods to create systems that account for human capabilities and limitations in aerospace environments.

The instructor will form teams based on each student's assessment of their interests and capabilities. Each team will select an aerospace human-system design project (e.g., a situational awareness display, rover controller, personal restraint system, payload workstation, etc.) and research the need for a solution, develop a proposed design, construct a prototype, and test or evaluate the prototype using the techniques and methods discussed in this course.

There will be several interim deliverables throughout the semester to ensure progress on the project. These include a design concept of operations, HSI design requirements, and human-in-the-loop testing and evaluation criteria. The final deliverables for the course project are a prototype, an oral presentation by the project team, and a final report. All team members must attend and participate in the presentation. Distance-learning students may pre-record their portion of the presentation or participate virtually, via Zoom, during the scheduled presentation. Additionally, there will be an award for the best design, as determined by an expert panel. The due dates for all deliverables are provided in the detailed course schedule.

Details regarding specific formats and requirements for all course project deliverables will be covered during lectures and posted on Canvas. Additionally, detailed grading rubrics for all deliverables will be provided and posted well in advance of the due dates. All students in the group will receive the same score on the project, unless indicated otherwise based on peer evaluations.

## Late Work Policy

Work submitted by a student as makeup work for an excused absence is not considered late work and is exempt from the late work policy (Student Rule 7).

## Course Specific Late Work Policy

Homework and project assignments submitted after the due date/time will not receive total credit, unless the delay is due to a university-excused absence per Student Rule 7. Points will be deducted for assignments submitted past the due date and time on Canvas-equivalent to 20% of the total points possible for each day, or portion thereof, past the due date. No late homework or project assignments will be accepted after 4 days.

Lecture activities may not be submitted late unless an extension has been granted due to a pre-approved university-excused absence.

## Course Schedule

A detailed course schedule, including homework assignment and project deliverable due dates is provided in Appendix A and posted on Canvas. Any updates to the schedule will be announced during lectures and through Canvas announcements.

### Course topics:

- Aerospace health and human performance risks

- Aerospace environments: Physical and cognitive stressors

- Aerospace human-system design process, including safety considerations

- Anthropometric considerations for spacecraft and aircraft

- Habitability considerations for long-duration space missions

- Cognitive workload, fatigue, attention, and situational awareness

- Aerospace vehicle designs: Displays & controls

- Physical/cognitive workload evaluation: physiological and subjective measures

- Human performance & usability evaluations

- Human reliability measures and human error mitigation strategies

- Human-system interface design for Extravehicular activity (EVA)

## Additional Course Information

Other resources:

The detailed lecture schedule, supplemental reading and reference material, lecture slides, and all homework and project assignments will be posted on course Canvas site. Reading the referenced material prior to viewing the lectures is essential in order to be prepared to effectively participate in class discussions.

### Discussion forums

Discussion forums for various topics will be provided on MS Teams will be used as a means for student collaborations and discussions.

### Re-grading Policy

Students have three days following the release of grades for an assignment or quiz to submit a re-grade request. The regrading request must be submitted in writing (not to exceed 1 page with 11-point font and single spacing). The request must clearly indicate the relevant problem(s) with the grade and justification for why re-grading is warranted.
